Sure, but you've abandoned Gwern's point now. Retreating from the motte will save your face but only by leaving Gwern out in the cold.

Consider the weather. Imperfect prediction of the weather has transformed society (and "the economy", whatever the fuck that is), but perfect prediction of the weather is impossible. The relevant limitation here is chaotic; even if we knew the positions of all atoms in the atmosphere, we will eventually be overwhelmed by the numerical effects of chaos. As a result, weather prediction beyond about two weeks is not physically realizable, regardless of implementation strategy. This two-week wall is known as the predictability barrier and it is a fundamental limitation of meteorology. Whether events are ergodic is not really relevant to the maths; even with a promise that atoms never return to their initial arrangements, the sheer size of the state space of the atmosphere will, by basic geometry, always be bigger than the amount of computation on Earth which we can assemble and bring to bear at the problem. Fun fact: chaos theory was discovered by meteorologists like Lorenz trying to figure out the correct differential equations for weather.

Think carefully. Your motte is that AI can magically turn chaotic systems into deterministic systems with simple-to-compute models; weather prediction is a counterexample. Retreating to the bailey, claiming that AI can magically initiate arbitrary societal transformations, doesn't work here because weather prediction is a counterexample to that, too; no AI will ever surmount this particular numerical obstacle, as a matter of computability theory.

text:
Previously, on Lobsters, we discussed Metamath, a system that is extremely amenable to proof search: in section 4.3 "The Anatomy of a Proof", p135, of the Metamath book, we can see that proofs are merely a sequence of instructions to apply to a stack along with a starting and ending configuration for the stack. A proof search is therefore a desired theorem (a desired start and end) along with a while-loop which repeatedly tries to apply every prior theorem to the top of each putative stack, returning success if it ever finds a stack which matches the ending configuration. There is a common question of how to self-apply this system; previously, on Lobsters we discussed Metamath Zero, which can describe itself at a low level and can be compiled to machine code. There is also a common question of whether this is the state of the art; previously, on Lobsters, the state of the art is that we can give a type signature and some objectives to a while-loop and have it genetically evolve candidates which incrementally approximate the desired properties.

The issue really is due to complexity theory and it is not a coincidence that computational complexity theory was first discovered by Gödel while wondering how to search for proofs. If you insist, perhaps thinking is required to come up with hypotheses which would make good theorems.

You're right that fair use is the main defense they're using, and it might hold up in court. But I don't think that makes licensing irrelevant, just not a standalone solution.

Licenses matter less as direct legal weapons right now and more as political and community signals. A “TGPL”-style license wouldn't immediately stop OpenAI, but it shifts the normative ground: it makes the extraction visible, names it as a violation of the spirit of open source, and gives future regulatory frameworks something to build on. GPL didn't work through constant litigation either; it worked by shaping expectations over time.

The fair use question also isn't fully settled. Some of the pending cases might go the other way. If they do, having clear license language in place already matters.

So yeah, licensing is one piece, not the whole answer. Which is why I listed it alongside regulatory and procurement approaches rather than treating it as sufficient on its own.

I think all the most important decisions in programming comes when coding in the small not when you're doing the overarching design, even when you're building a big system. The big design rarely contains anything novel and is mostly only a way to partition the work into pieces that is tractable to implement separately. Back in the 90s it was unfashionable to do the actual implementation work on these modules, the vision was that architects would give grunt programmers UML diagrams and that the implementation would be mechanical uncreative work. CASE tools such as Rational was a big deal.

There was a great resistance to these ideas at the time (read Joel on Software about architecture astronauts or The Pragmatic Programmer), and it turns out that the CASE visions were wrongheaded. In the same manner I think abdicating all the detail work to AI models are exactly as wrongheaded. The tactical decisions are the important decisions, and you can't build quality software without being involved with them.

text:
I think this somewhat uncritically equivocates two behaviors.

IDE autocompletes (specifically those which do not generate code, but do generate syntactic elements, e.g., closing braces) and refactorings affect the syntax of a program. You don't defer your semantic choices in this case.

Code generators (regardless of how that code is generated; code synthesis, boilerplate generators, etc. are relevant here too) affect the semantics of a program. When you use these, you defer responsibility/quality/correctness/etc. to the generator you use. Yes, you can review it, but that is nowhere near the level of care nor the procedural consideration that it takes to write it.

Whether you are writing the code or reviewing it, you will suffer decision fatigue. When you're writing the code, this might make you take a break or choose easier, less optimal implementations; after all, you won't write effective or necessarily correct code in this case. But ultimately, you are still responsible for actually producing the code, so you will manage your decision fatigue s.t. you can still write reasonable code. When you're reviewing code, you will engage in avoidant or complacent behavior that leads you to review less carefully. This is a well-understood psychological phenomenon (habituation of acceptance, normalization of deviance, etc.). The reason I consider "code generation + review" as vibecoding is simple: you defer responsibility to the LLM for the semantics of your program and you will, necessarily, become complacent in accepting its output. The degree to which the LLM is able to transform your prompt containing your natural-language semantics into code is somewhat irrelevant, because there is always more detail in code than you can encode in a prompt (and, if there wasn't, it would be just as costly to write a prompt as it would be to write the code).

text:
Sure, I should definitely write this up properly at some point!

The basic idea behind my workflow is that writing code isn't the real bottleneck. The real bottleneck is understanding the problem and the code. So anything that generates code faster than I can understand it is a problem. So agent swarms are mostly useless, because they speed up code generation without improving understanding. Asking an agent to look at my code and see if I've overlooked anything, on the other hand, increases my understanding. Especially if I do the fixes myself.

Now, it's also important that not all code requires equal understanding. Just like on human projects, there are parts I don't care too much about, and parts that I watch like a hawk. Knowing which part is which is where experience helps. The core Rust traits in a system are very important. The 9th implementation of some trait may not be.

Similarly, I choose my models carefully. My model needs to be smart enough to debug a broken library, or to help me figure out mathematical invariants for a prop test. But it shouldn't be so smart that I'm tempted to let it do a lot of work unsupervised. Somewhere between Sonnet 4.5 and Opus 4.6 is ideal. Fable is too smart. In practice, this means running open models like Qwen3.8 27B, Qwen3.8 Flash Next, or DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731. These are all smart enough to walk me through the interaction of two monads (say, flatMap and propFlatMap) if I ask. But they're not smart enough to encourage true vibecoding and "not even reading the code." Probably the largest I would consider for my own work is GLM 5.3 Flash, but you have to be really rich to run it locally.

My favorite agent harness is Pi. One session, no background agents, no TODO list, no plan mode, no fancy workflows. Maybe 1,500 tokens in my AGENTS.md, plus 2 or 3 tiny skills that tell the agent how I like to break down problems. (Which I do not share publicly, because I don't want future agents to learn how I break down problems.)

For version control, I use jj. Using it really well isn't any simpler than learning git. But it makes it easy to break up changes into multiple tiny pieces, and then interactively edit any of those pieces. I have some skills telling the agent to "break changes up Linux kernel style," and how to write a good commit message. This allows me to review tiny, standalone pieces right in Zed and edit patch 3 of 4 all that I want.

I still invest time in my editor. I'm trying Zed these days, with Zeta2 as a code completion model. Zeta2 is nice, because it only completes obvious things, and it rarely completes more than 3 lines. If it has any doubt, it moves my cursor to the part I need to fill in. I work in Rust whenever I can, because I like Rust. And I very regularly drop into my editor and rough out traits, refactor things, and think with my fingers.

Overall, this process is good because it maximizes my understanding. And once a project passes 3,000 lines, a deeper understanding helps me move faster. Like, I started programming on the Apple IIe, and I like to imagine I've gotten pretty decent at it. Plus, it's fun. Letting an agent write all the code would be like letting an agent go watch a fun movie for me.

But the north star of this process is that I'm optimizing for understanding, not speed. And from there, everything else is just making deliberate choices. My process has actually gotten more minimalist with time. And as agents have gotten smarter, I've become increasingly alienated from frontier models. I want a model that will punish me swiftly for trying to delegate too much understanding. It's sort of like my kayak: It's quite maneuverable, but it punishes sloppy technique by making me swim.

This is not the only process I use. Sometimes I just turn the agents off entirely, or limit them to research. But at its best, this understanding-focused process is like having a smart pair programmer or a faculty advisor. I can ask it for tips on what I'm overlooking, or I can say, "I don't really feel like converting from the old Rust error handling library to the new one, so please do that for me." But at each step, I focus on maintaining understanding. And if I do lose understanding, I also lose productivity.

text:
These are good observations about "the split".

It wasn't apparent to me before the advent of LLMs that many of my colleagues think very differently about software. Obviously, the primary goal of software is to Do Thing, but to me, a lot of the satisfaction of my job comes from kneading the code until it's as streamlined, simple and elegant as I can make it while accumulating a thorough understanding of the entire system.

I don't like how coding agents disconnect me from that process.

text:
This is also what I find most enjoyable about software engineering. I want the code to actually be good, even in ways that are intangible and highly subjective.

But I find LLM agents an effective tool for accomplishing that because I actually edit the code after them. Refactoring their "soft clay" code into something actually good is easier, faster, and more enjoyable for me than operating from a blank page. I can leave some sections "sketched" - with mediocre LLM code - and come back to them later while I focus on other things. I can quickly explore ideas and find out where they go wrong, or incorporate algorithms I don't know well by editing from an implementation in a language I do, instead of translating from psuedocode in a paper. I feel like my ability to write good code is massively unlocked by LLMs, not disconnected.

You don't have to use agents to "vibecode" an entire app with your eyes closed. I don't understand why the discussion about this technology is stuck in a rut framed around a single use practice.
